answers: A thread pool sized to the cores
writing.exampleCaption: Ten thousand of these is routine; ten thousand threads is not.
writing.explanation:
A thread costs a stack and a scheduler slot, which is fine for a few hundred and painful for a hundred thousand. Async tasks are state machines sharing a small pool of threads, so waiting on ten thousand sockets is cheap — but a task that computes without yielding blocks everything sharing its thread. The dividing line is whether the work waits or works.

A thread is an operating-system execution context; an async task is a future that an executor polls. The async task can yield during nonblocking waits, allowing one thread to serve many waiting operations. A thread can execute CPU work in parallel with other threads when cores are available. These distinctions are more useful than saying one technology is for all I/O and the other for all CPU. Small systems may use threads for I/O perfectly well, and async applications still use threads underneath.

Imagine ten thousand mostly idle connections. One thread per connection can consume considerable stack reservation and scheduling overhead; an async runtime can represent each wait as compact task state and wake only ready work. Now imagine image compression that runs for a second without yielding. Put it directly on an executor worker and other tasks sharing that worker wait. Offload CPU-heavy or blocking work to an appropriate pool, with a bound on how much can queue.

For an interview, ask what the workload does while it is not producing results. If it waits on sockets, choose an async I/O model or another scalable event-driven design. If it computes, decide how many cores and jobs are available and use threads or a compute pool. Add cancellation and shutdown to the answer: a detached task can outlive a request, while a thread needs a join or explicit lifecycle. Measure latency and memory under representative load rather than repeating one universal task-count threshold.
